cards.explanation: The answer is to pray at all times and not lose heart. Luke tells us Jesus spoke this parable “…about their need to pray at all times and not lose heart…” (Luke 18:1). The point comes first, before a single character walks on stage. Keep praying, friends, and keep your heart in it.

The answer is False. The text says "For a while he refused, but later he said to himself…" (Luke 18:4). So the widow didn't win on her first try. She kept appealing to him, and the judge's mind changed later.

The word is pestering. The judge says it himself: "…because this widow keeps pestering me, I will give her justice." (Luke 18:5). He doesn't say he suddenly cared. She kept coming, and he decided to give her justice.

The answer is day and night, friends. Jesus asks, "Will not God bring about justice for His elect who cry out to Him day and night?" (Luke 18:7). That's no once-in-a-while cry. It keeps going, morning and midnight.
The word is promptly. Jesus says, "I tell you, He will promptly carry out justice on their behalf." (Luke 18:8). He asks first whether God will delay in helping them. Then He answers: promptly.

The answer is True. Jesus closes with a question: "Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on earth?" (Luke 18:8). "…Son of Man…" is the name Jesus uses for Himself (Mark 2:10). I don't know when that day is, and Matthew 24:36 says only the Father does. That's why my ovens stay ready.

The word is righteousness. Jesus told this parable “To some who trusted in their own righteousness and viewed others with contempt…” (Luke 18:9). Those two things come together in the same sentence. I'm listening closely, friends.

The other man is a tax collector. The text says, "Two men went up to the temple to pray. One was a Pharisee and the other a tax collector." (Luke 18:10). Two men, one temple, and two very different prayers on the way.

The Pharisee thanks God that he is not like other men. He says: “God, I thank You that I am not like other men…” (Luke 18:11). He starts with thanks, but the thanks is about how he compares to everybody else. He even brings up the tax collector, saying “…or even like this tax collector.” (Luke 18:11). I'd call that a thank-you with a side-eye.
The answer is False. His next words are, "I fast twice a week and pay tithes of all that I acquire." (Luke 18:12). He tells God what he does. He doesn't confess a single sin.

The tax collector prays, "God, have mercy on me, a sinner!" (Luke 18:13). Eyes down, hand on his chest, and one short, honest sentence. I think the shortest prayer in the story is the one that says the most.

The answer is True. Jesus says, "I tell you, this man, rather than the Pharisee, went home justified." (Luke 18:14). The man who beat his breast and asked for mercy is the one who went home justified. That's the twist, and Jesus Himself gives it.

The word is exalted. Jesus says, "For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted." (Luke 18:14). Lift yourself up and you get brought down. Stay low, and you get lifted. I learned that from a drawer, friends.
